https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/02.subtitle: British artist's Expedition in Pursuit of Rare Meats was criticised as offensive in wake of Black Lives Matter protests
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2022/02.text:
British painter Rex Whistler's “racist” mural at Tate Britain will remain in place, the gallery has confirmed, with trustees determined to keep the artwork despite the controversy surrounding it.
The 1927 work The Expedition in Pursuit of Rare Meats, containing images of black children bound in rope, was condemned for containing “racist imagery” in the wake of Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, and was deemed “offensive” by the Tate’s ethics committee.
The offensiveness of the mural was made worse by its location in the Tate’s “Rex Whistler Restaurant”, it was said, and the high-end eatery was closed to the public while the future of the off-limits artwork inside it was reviewed.
The mural will remain in place and on display, the gallery has announced, but the restaurant will be closed to ensure that it can be seen in a more “inclusive” context. A new artwork will be commissioned to “critically engage with the mural’s history and content, including its racist imagery”, Tate bosses said.
Whistler, famed for his high-society portraiture, painted the fantastical landscape of The Expedition when he was 23 years old.
The mural, telling the story of a hunt for exotic meats, is regarded as one of his most important works, but contains images of black children on leads and caricatured Chinese characters.
It is understood legislation protecting publicly owned art would have prevented the piece from being removed completely.
Alex Farquharson, the director of Tate Britain, said: “The Rex Whistler mural presents a unique challenge. The mural is part of our institutional and cultural history and we must take responsibility for it, but this new approach will also enable us to reflect on the values and commitments we hold today.”
In September 2020, members of the Tate’s ethics committee were “unequivocal in their view that the imagery of the work is offensive”, and that the offensiveness of its depictions of black people as hunted slaves was made worse by its display in the restaurant.
Descendants of Whistler, a British artist who was killed in action in France in 1944 at the age of 39, said at the time that it was “unsurprising” that a “work of the past” contained potentially outdated imagery which posed a problem for the Tate.
The gallery brought in outside experts to help arrive at the decision on the future of the mural, considered one of his most important works, and how to address its “power” in a “historically white institution”.
Amia Srinivasan, a professor of social and political theory at All Souls College, University of Oxford, and a co-chairman of Rex Whistler mural discussions, said:  “Conversations about the mural were open, rigorous, and filled with good-natured but deep disagreement.
“Would keeping the mural open to the public accentuate its power? Would shutting it off risk doing the same? Could the space be used by artists of colour as a creative site of reappropriation? Or would this unfairly burden them with a problem produced by a historically white institution?
“One of the few points of consensus was that Tate had to take ownership of its history, and that whatever decision was made had to be an invitation to a broader conversation, not the end of one.”
The artist who will create the piece to work critically with Whistler’s mural is yet to be decided.
